conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. My name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the EPDS, which screens for depressive and anxiety symptoms that can sometimes show up after childbirth, including a question about thoughts of self-harm.  

The purpose is simply to get a snapshot of how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days so we can be sure you’re getting the right support. Everything you share here is confidential, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no right or wrong answers, only your honest experience.

We’ll go through 10 questions together; I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, just let me know and we can pause.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to look forward to things, or have you noticed that you’re not really feeling enjoyment or interest in the moments that used to make you smile?

[soft sigh, eyes a little glassy]

It’s… well, it’s mostly gone. I used to get excited about the littlest things—like my morning coffee while I watched the sun come up, or texting my best friend stupid memes—but now even when I try to do those, it feels flat. The only thing that still gives me a flicker is when my baby gives me that sleepy milk-grin, but even that pleasure feels muffled, like it’s coming through a thick blanket.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[small shrug, forcing a half-smile]

Not really… I mean, every now and then something will catch me off-guard and I’ll sort of chuckle, but it’s over fast and it doesn’t feel the same. Mostly I’m just too tired or worried to find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[looking down at my hands]

Hardly at all. Even when my partner says, “Let’s order your favorite take-out tonight,” I just feel… nothing. I tell myself I *should* look forward to it, but it’s like the switch that makes things feel exciting is broken. The only thing I half look forward to is the few minutes when the baby is asleep and the house is quiet—but even that’s more relief than real enjoyment.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[Voice drops, fingers twist the edge of my sweater]

Yeah... a lot. If he spits up more than usual, my head goes straight to "I must've eaten something wrong." When he wouldn't settle last night, I kept thinking, "Other moms know how to calm their babies—why can't I figure it out?" It feels like every hiccup is somehow my fault, even when my partner says it's normal baby stuff.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[exhales shakily]

Pretty much all the time. My heart races the second I hear him make any noise—like, what if he stopped breathing? Sometimes I'll just stare at his chest to be sure it's moving, or I'll lie in bed imagining the crib tipping over, or the dog barking and waking him, or... I know it sounds crazy, but I can't switch the thoughts off. There's no real danger, yet my body feels like there's an alarm going off 24/7.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[nods slowly, arms crossed tight over my chest]

Yes... a few times this week it hit me out of nowhere. My heart starts pounding and I feel like I can't get a full breath, even if the baby's fine and the room is quiet. Once, my partner found me standing over the crib just shaking, and I couldn't explain why—nothing had happened. It feels like a wave of dread rushing in with no warning, and I have to pace or rock myself to make it pass.
Things have been getting on top of me

[Voice cracks a little, eyes welling]

Yeah... most days I feel like I'm drowning in little tasks. Feed, burp, change, try to nap—then the cycle starts again, and somehow there's still laundry everywhere and dishes in the sink. I'll look at the mess and just freeze, thinking, "How does everyone else keep up?" Sometimes I end up crying while I'm folding onesies because it feels like I'm failing at the simplest stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]

Yes... I lie down exhausted, but my head won't stop spinning. I replay every tiny thing I did that day—did I hold him the right way, did I miss a feeding cue?—and the worry just loops. It takes me forever to drift off, and when I finally do, I jerk awake thinking I heard him cry. Even when my partner takes the night shift, I wake up every couple of hours with my heart racing, sure something's wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

[eyes water, voice small]

A lot of the time. It’s like a heavy cloud settled over me. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly feel this wave of sadness, like I’m doing everything I’m supposed to and still feel empty. Some afternoons I just sit on the couch with him asleep on my chest, crying quietly because I miss the version of me who used to feel light.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[sniffs, wipes cheek with sleeve]

Yeah... it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday I dropped a clean burp cloth on the floor and just burst into tears—couldn’t even explain why. It’s like the tears are sitting right behind my eyes all day, and any tiny thing tips them over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[fidgets with the hem of my shirt, voice barely above a whisper]

Once or twice... just brief flashes. Like, I'll be rocking him at 3 a.m., totally spent, and this quick image pops in—"what if I just kept walking out the door and didn't come back?" I never planned anything, and I don't want to leave him... but the thought flickered there for a second before I shoved it away and felt horrible for even thinking it.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has faded, replaced by near-constant worry, guilt, and a heavy sadness that makes even small tasks feel impossible. Despite loving your baby and trying your best, you're exhausted, tearful, and sometimes frightened by your own thoughts. Your honesty shows remarkable strength, and it's clear you want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, fleeting laughter that feels diminished and joyless, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Hardly at all" and describes complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>She describes frequent self-blame ("a lot," "every hiccup is somehow my fault") matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant, intrusive worries and physical anxiety symptoms 'all the time' with no rational basis, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms (heart pounding, breathlessness, shaking) and dread, indicating frequent occurrences.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage basic tasks, tearful, and perceives herself as failing—clearly matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly worry loops preventing sleep onset, repeated wakings due to anxiety, and persistent racing thoughts—meets "Yes, most of the time" severity.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness most afternoons and frequent tears, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying twice this week from minor triggers, indicating frequent tearfulness consistent with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS=26 (≥14 plus Item 10=1) places you in the high-risk range. You describe <sym>daily low mood</sym>, complete loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>heightened anxiety</sym> with panic symptoms, <sym>sleep disruption</sym> from racing thoughts, and <sym>fleeting escape ideas</sym>. These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about <med>evidence-based therapy</med> (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and <med>sertraline</med> (first-line antidepressant while breastfeeding)
3. Plan brief safety check-ins with your partner until professional review; keep local 24-h crisis line handy
4. Encourage 15-min outdoor daylight walks and accept help with night feeds to protect 4-hour sleep blocks
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to gauge treatment response
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
(Responses to 10-item EPDS-equivalent)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent tearfulness  
- Marked loss of enjoyment (even preferred activities)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Intrusive, unrealistic anxiety and catastrophic worries  
- Panic episodes (physical arousal, shortness of breath)  
- Feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope with daily tasks  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to racing thoughts  
- Passive, transient thoughts of self-harm / leaving (no plan)

Pattern  
Consistent with moderate–severe depressive and anxious symptomatology arising in postpartum period; functional impairment significant.

Safety  
Self-harm ideation reported (passive, no intent or plan) → elevated risk; requires immediate safety assessment and monitoring.

Screening conclusion  
High clinical concern for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; formal diagnostic evaluation and safety planning indicated.
